title: Contentment, Money and Staying True
overview: Paul closes his letter to Timothy with instructions on slaves and masters, warnings about teachers who use religion to get rich, and a call to contentment, generosity and faithfulness.

parts.label: Slaves and their masters (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Christian slaves in Roman households are told to respect their masters, even believing ones, so the new faith would not be mocked as a cause of disorder. The letter does not challenge slavery itself, and many readers today find these verses troubling, especially since they were later used to defend slavery.

parts.label: Teachers who argue for profit (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Paul describes teachers who reject the plain teaching tied to Jesus and instead love endless arguments over words, which breed envy, suspicion and constant friction. Worse, they treat religion as a way to make money.

parts.label: Enough is real wealth (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Paul turns their idea around: faith joined with being satisfied with enough is the real gain, since we arrive with nothing and leave with nothing. It is the craving to be rich, not money itself, that he calls a root of many kinds of evil, one that leads people away from faith and into deep pain.

parts.label: A charge to Timothy (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Timothy is told to run from greed and chase goodness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness, holding to the public commitment he once made, which may mean his baptism or his appointment as a leader; scholars are unsure. Paul links this to Jesus standing firm before Pilate, then breaks into praise of God as the one true ruler, living in light no one can approach.

parts.label: Advice for the wealthy (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: The rich are not told to give everything up, but to avoid arrogance and not to trust in wealth that can vanish. They are to be generous and quick to share, which Paul says builds a lasting foundation and leads to the life that is truly life.

parts.label: Guard what you were given (vv. 20-21)
parts.note: Timothy is to protect the message entrusted to him and steer clear of empty talk that claims to offer special, deeper knowledge. Some scholars connect this to early ideas that later grew into movements promising secret knowledge, though exactly what Paul had in mind is uncertain.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these warnings about money call for a simple, modest way of living or mainly for a right attitude and generosity while keeping one's wealth.
think: What would having enough look like in your own life, and what makes that line hard to draw?
